flashcards.title: Set Definitions and Types
formulas: A set is a well-defined collection of objects.
A set is described either in set builder form or tabular form.
A null set (Ø) has no elements.
A singleton set contains a single element.
A finite set has a definite number of elements; otherwise, it is infinite.
explanation: A set is defined as a collection of distinct objects.
Sets can be represented using specific notation methods.
A null set has no elements and is represented as Ø.
A singleton set consists of exactly one element.
Finite sets have a countable number of elements, while infinite sets do not.

flashcards.title: Set Operations and Subsets
formulas: If A and B are sets, A is a subset of B if every element of A is also in B.
Union: A ∪ B = {x: x ∈ A or x ∈ B}.
Intersection: A ∩ B = {x: x ∈ A and x ∈ B}.
Difference: A - B = {x: x ∈ A and x ∉ B}.
Complement: A' = {x: x ∈ U and x ∉ A}.
explanation: A subset means all elements of one set are contained in another.
Union combines elements from two sets.
Intersection finds common elements between two sets.
Difference finds elements present in one set but not in another.
Complement identifies elements in the universal set not in the given set.

flashcards.title: Intervals and Power Sets
formulas: Closed interval: [a, b] = {x: a ≤ x ≤ b}.
Open interval: (a, b) = {x: a < x < b}.
Semi-open interval: [a, b) = {x: a ≤ x < b}.
Power set: P(A) = 2^n, where n is the number of elements in A.
explanation: Intervals define a range of real numbers with specific inclusions.
Closed intervals include the endpoints, open intervals exclude them.
Semi-open intervals include one endpoint but not the other.
The power set of a set includes all its possible subsets.

flashcards.title: Laws of Sets
formulas: Idempotent laws: A ∪ A = A and A ∩ A = A.
Identity laws: A ∪ Ø = A and A ∩ U = A.
Commutative laws: A ∪ B = B ∪ A and A ∩ B = B ∩ A.
Associative laws: (A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C) and (A ∩ B) ∩ C = A ∩ (B ∩ C).
Distributive laws: A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C) and A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).
De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.
explanation: Idempotent laws state that combining a set with itself results in the same set.
Identity laws describe the effect of null and universal sets on union and intersection.
Commutative laws show that the order of union or intersection doesn't matter.
Associative laws allow grouping without affecting union or intersection results.
Distributive laws explain the interaction between union and intersection.
De Morgan's laws provide rules for complements of unions and intersections.

flashcards.title: Relations Basics and Cartesian Product
formulas: An ordered pair consists of two objects in a fixed order.
Cartesian product: A × B = {(a, b): a ∈ A, b ∈ B}.
If A and B have m and n elements respectively, A × B has m × n elements.
R = {(x, y): x, y ∈ R} defines all points in the xy-plane.
explanation: An ordered pair is a combination of two elements with a specific sequence.
Equality in ordered pairs requires both elements to match in order.
The Cartesian product combines every element of one set with every element of another.
The number of elements in the Cartesian product equals the product of the sizes of the two sets.
The set of all (x, y) points represents the xy-plane.

flashcards.title: Set Operations in Relations
formulas: A × (B − C) = A × B − A × C.
If A = B, then A × B = B × A.
explanation: Union in Cartesian products is distributive.
Intersection in Cartesian products is distributive.
Difference in Cartesian products follows the same distributive property.
If two sets are equal, their Cartesian product with each other is symmetric.
The intersection of Cartesian products depends on the intersections of individual sets.
Distributive properties hold for Cartesian products and unions.

flashcards.title: Relations and Domain/Range
formulas: A relation from A to B is a subset of A × B.
If A and B are finite with m and n elements, there are 2^(m×n) possible relations.
Domain(R) = {x: (x, y) ∈ R}.
Range(R) = {y: (x, y) ∈ R}.
Inverse relation R⁻¹ = {(b, a): (a, b) ∈ R}.
explanation: A relation links elements of one set to another based on specific conditions.
The number of possible relations depends on the size of the Cartesian product.
The domain of a relation is the set of all first elements.
The range of a relation is the set of all second elements.
The inverse of a relation swaps the order of elements in the pairs.

flashcards.title: Functions
formulas: A relation f from A to B is a function if for each a ∈ A, there exists a unique b ∈ B such that (a, b) ∈ f.
Domain of f: Set A.
Co-domain of f: Set B.
Range of f: The set of all images of elements in the domain.
explanation: A function ensures that each input has a unique output.
The domain is the set of all possible inputs to the function.
The co-domain is the set containing all possible outputs.
The range is the actual set of outputs generated by the function.

flashcards.title: Fundamental Trigonometric Identities
formulas: sin x = 1/cosec x or cosec x = 1/sin x
cos x = 1/sec x or sec x = 1/cos x
cot x = 1/tan x or tan x = 1/cot x
tan x = sin x / cos x or cot x = cos x / sin x
sin²x + cos²x = 1
1 + tan²x = sec²x or sec²x - tan²x = 1
1 + cot²x = cosec²x or cosec²x - cot²x = 1
explanation: These equations define the reciprocal relationships between basic trigonometric functions.
The Pythagorean identities relate sin, cos, tan, and sec to fundamental properties of a right triangle.
Equations for tangent and cotangent are derived from sine and cosine.

flashcards.title: Negative Angle Identities
formulas: sin(-x) = -sin x or cosec(-x) = -cosec x
cos(-x) = cos x or sec(-x) = sec x
tan(-x) = -tan x or cot(-x) = -cot x
explanation: These formulas show how trigonometric functions behave for negative angles.
Sine, tangent, and cosecant are odd functions, meaning they change sign with a negative angle.
Cosine and secant are even functions, meaning their value remains the same for negative angles.

flashcards.title: Supplementary Angle Identities
formulas: sin(π/2 - x) = cos x or cos(π/2 - x) = sin x
tan(π/2 - x) = cot x or cot(π/2 - x) = tan x
sec(π/2 - x) = cosec x or cosec(π/2 - x) = sec x
explanation: These identities relate trigonometric functions of complementary angles (adding up to 90° or π/2 radians).
The roles of sine and cosine, tangent and cotangent, secant and cosecant are interchanged.

flashcards.title: Periodicity and Even/Odd Properties
formulas: sin(2π - x) = -sin x, cos(2π - x) = cos x
tan(2π - x) = -tan x, cot(2π - x) = -cot x
sec(2π - x) = sec x, cosec(2π - x) = -cosec x
Sine and Cosine are periodic with period 2π.
Tangent and Cotangent are periodic with period π.
Cosine and secant are even functions; others are odd functions.
explanation: These identities describe periodic behavior of trigonometric functions over their respective periods.
Even functions remain unchanged with a negative angle, while odd functions invert their sign.

flashcards.title: Definition of a Statement
formulas: A sentence or description which can be judged to be true or false is called a statement.
Statements involving mathematical relations are called mathematical statements.
explanation: A statement is a logical sentence that can be evaluated as either true or false.
Mathematical statements specifically involve relationships or expressions in mathematics.

flashcards.title: First Principle of Mathematical Induction
formulas: Let P(n) be a statement involving the natural number n such that:
(i) P(1) is true.
(ii) P(m + 1) is true whenever P(m) is true.
Then, P(n) is true for all n ∈ N.
explanation: Defines the assumption of P(n) being a statement involving natural numbers.
The base case ensures that the first step, P(1), is true.
This proves that if P(m) is true, then P(m + 1) is also true.
Concludes that P(n) is true for all natural numbers.

flashcards.title: Second Principle of Mathematical Induction
formulas: Let P(n) be a statement involving the natural number n such that:
(i) P(1) is true.
(ii) P(m + 1) is true whenever P(n) is true for all n ≤ m.
Then, P(n) is true for all n ∈ N.
explanation: Defines the assumption of P(n) involving natural numbers for the second principle.
The base case ensures that the first step, P(1), is true.
Extends the assumption to cover all previous values (n ≤ m).
Concludes that P(n) is true for all natural numbers using this principle.

flashcards.title: Complex Numbers - Basics
formulas: √(-1) is an imaginary quantity denoted by i, and i² = -1.
For any positive real number a, √a = a^(1/2).
If a, b are real numbers, √(a + b) = √a + √b, provided at least one of a or b is positive.
explanation: The imaginary unit i is the foundation of complex numbers.
Square roots of positive numbers can be expressed as fractional exponents.
Square root operations involving addition are valid under specific conditions.

flashcards.title: Complex Numbers - Definitions
formulas: A complex number z = a + ib, where a is the real part and b is the imaginary part.
z is purely real if Im(z) = 0.
z is purely imaginary if Re(z) = 0.
explanation: A complex number consists of a real part and an imaginary part.
A purely real complex number has no imaginary component.
A purely imaginary complex number has no real component.

flashcards.title: Operations on Complex Numbers
formulas: Addition: z₁ + z₂ = (a₁ + a₂) + i(b₁ + b₂).
Subtraction: z₁ - z₂ = (a₁ - a₂) + i(b₁ - b₂).
Multiplication: z₁ * z₂ = (a₁a₂ - b₁b₂) + i(a₁b₂ + a₂b₁).
Division: z₁ / z₂ = [(a₁a₂ + b₁b₂) / (a₂² + b₂²)] + i[(b₁a₂ - a₁b₂) / (a₂² + b₂²)].
explanation: Addition combines the real and imaginary parts of the two numbers.
Subtraction works similarly to addition but subtracts corresponding components.
Multiplication involves both real and imaginary cross terms.
Division uses the conjugate of the denominator to simplify the fraction.

flashcards.title: Quadratic Equations - Roots
formulas: Roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 are given by: α = [-b + √D] / 2a, β = [-b - √D] / 2a.
Discriminant D = b² - 4ac.
If D > 0, roots are real and distinct.
If D = 0, roots are real and equal.
If D < 0, roots are complex conjugates.
explanation: The quadratic formula gives the roots of a second-degree equation.
The discriminant determines the nature of the roots.
Positive D indicates distinct real roots.
Zero D results in equal real roots.
Negative D yields complex conjugate roots.

flashcards.title: Basics of Linear Inequalities
formulas: A linear inequality in one variable is of the form ax + b > 0, ax + b < 0, ax + b ≥ 0, or ax + b ≤ 0.
A linear inequality in two variables is of the form ax + by + c > 0, ax + by + c < 0, ax + by + c ≥ 0, or ax + by + c ≤ 0.
Solution of a linear inequality in one variable is a set of real numbers satisfying the inequality.
Solution of a linear inequality in two variables is a region in the Cartesian plane.
explanation: Linear inequalities are expressions with inequalities instead of equality.
In two variables, the solution is a half-plane above or below the line.
Solutions in one variable are intervals on the number line.
For two variables, shading represents the solution region on the graph.

flashcards.title: Rules of Linear Inequalities
formulas: If a > b, then a + c > b + c for any c.
If a > b, then a - c > b - c for any c.
If a > b and c > 0, then ac > bc.
If a > b and c < 0, then ac < bc.
explanation: Adding the same number to both sides of an inequality preserves it.
Subtracting the same number from both sides of an inequality preserves it.
Multiplying by a positive number preserves the inequality.
Multiplying by a negative number reverses the inequality.

flashcards.title: Graphical Representation of Linear Inequalities
formulas: To graph ax + by + c > 0 or ax + by + c < 0, first plot the line ax + by + c = 0.
Choose a test point not on the line to determine which side satisfies the inequality.
For ax + by + c ≥ 0 or ax + by + c ≤ 0, include the line itself in the solution.
The solution region is shaded based on the inequality.
explanation: The line ax + by + c = 0 divides the plane into two regions.
A test point (usually (0, 0) if not on the line) helps identify the solution region.
For '≥' or '≤', the boundary line is part of the solution.
Shading indicates the valid region for the inequality.

flashcards.title: System of Linear Inequalities
formulas: The solution of a system of linear inequalities is the region common to all individual solutions.
Graph each inequality and find the intersection of their solution regions.
The region may be bounded or unbounded depending on the inequalities.
For real-life problems, the feasible region often represents possible solutions.
explanation: Solving multiple inequalities together involves finding overlap in solutions.
Each inequality contributes to shaping the feasible region.
The solution region is the intersection of all individual inequality regions.
Applications include optimization problems and resource allocation.

flashcards.title: Basics of Permutations
formulas: The product of the first n natural numbers is called n factorial: n! = 1 × 2 × 3 × ... × (n - 1) × n.
Factorials of proper fractions and negative integers are not defined.
n! + 1 is not divisible by any natural number between 2 and n.
For a prime number p and natural number n, Ep(n) = [n/p] + [n/p²] + [n/p³] + ...
explanation: n factorial (n!) is the total number of ways to arrange n distinct items.
Factorials are only defined for non-negative integers.
This property shows the uniqueness of factorial sums plus one.
Ep(n) denotes the exponent of a prime number in n! (factorial).

flashcards.title: Basics of Combinations
formulas: If n is a natural number and r is a non-negative integer such that 0 ≤ r ≤ n: nCr = n! / [r!(n - r)!].
nCr × r! = nPr, where nPr = n! / (n - r)!.
nCr + nC(r - 1) = n+1Cr.
nCr = nC(n - r).
explanation: nCr represents the number of ways to choose r items from n distinct items.
The relation between permutations and combinations helps compute results.
This property allows combinations to be recursively calculated.
Combinations are symmetric: choosing r items is the same as excluding n - r items.

flashcards.title: Special Properties of Combinations
formulas: If n is an even natural number, the greatest among nC0, nC1, ..., nCn is nC(n/2).
If n is an odd natural number, the greatest among nC0, nC1, ..., nCn is either nC(n//2) or nC(n//2 + 1).
The number of ways to select r items from n distinct items is given by nCr = n! / [r!(n - r)!].
explanation: For even n, the central combination is the greatest.
For odd n, the greatest combination lies around the midpoint.
This formula is the foundation for calculating combinations.

flashcards.title: Applications of Permutations and Combinations
formulas: Number of permutations of n items taken r at a time: nPr = n! / (n - r)!.
Number of combinations of n items taken r at a time: nCr = n! / [r!(n - r)!].
Total subsets of a set with n elements: 2^n.
Number of permutations of n items where items are repeated: n! / (p1! × p2! × ... × pk!).
explanation: Permutations count the number of ordered arrangements.
Combinations count the number of unordered selections.
The total subsets include all combinations of a set.
This formula accounts for repetitions in permutations.

flashcards.title: Basics of Sequences
formulas: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers written as {a₁, a₂, a₃, ...}.
Finite sequence: A sequence with a finite number of terms.
Infinite sequence: A sequence with an infinite number of terms.
General term of a sequence: aₙ = f(n), where n is the position of the term.
explanation: A sequence is a set of numbers arranged in a specific order.
Finite sequences have a specific last term.
Infinite sequences continue indefinitely without a final term.
The general term represents a rule to find any term in the sequence.

flashcards.title: Arithmetic Progression (AP)
formulas: An AP is a sequence where the difference between consecutive terms is constant.
nth term of an AP: aₙ = a + (n-1)d.
Sum of the first n terms of an AP: Sₙ = (n/2)[2a + (n-1)d].
Sum of the first n terms (alternative): Sₙ = (n/2)(a + l), where l is the last term.
explanation: In an AP, the difference between two consecutive terms is called the common difference (d).
The nth term formula helps find any term in the AP.
The sum formula calculates the total of the first n terms.
An alternative formula can be used if the last term is known.

flashcards.title: Geometric Progression (GP)
formulas: A GP is a sequence where the ratio between consecutive terms is constant.
nth term of a GP: aₙ = ar^(n-1).
Sum of the first n terms of a GP (r ≠ 1): Sₙ = a(1 - rⁿ) / (1 - r).
Sum of an infinite GP (|r| < 1): S = a / (1 - r).
explanation: In a GP, the ratio between consecutive terms is called the common ratio (r).
The nth term formula helps find any term in the GP.
The sum formula calculates the total of the first n terms for r ≠ 1.
For an infinite GP with |r| < 1, the sum converges to a specific value.

flashcards.title: Relationship Between AM, GM, and HM
formulas: Arithmetic Mean (AM): AM = (a + b) / 2.
Geometric Mean (GM): GM = √(ab).
Harmonic Mean (HM): HM = 2ab / (a + b).
Relationship: AM ≥ GM ≥ HM.
explanation: AM is the average of two numbers.
GM is the square root of the product of two numbers.
HM is the reciprocal of the average of the reciprocals of two numbers.
AM, GM, and HM follow an inequality relationship.

flashcards.title: Special Series
formulas: Sum of first n natural numbers: Sₙ = n(n + 1) / 2.
Sum of squares of first n natural numbers: Sₙ = n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 6.
Sum of cubes of first n natural numbers: Sₙ = [n(n + 1) / 2]².
explanation: The sum of natural numbers gives the total of the first n positive integers.
The sum of squares calculates the total of the squares of the first n natural numbers.
The sum of cubes is the square of the sum of the first n natural numbers.

flashcards.title: Basics of Straight Lines
formulas: Every first-degree equation in x and y represents a straight line.
The slope of a non-vertical line passing through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is m = (y₂ - y₁) / (x₂ - x₁).
Slope of a horizontal line = 0, and slope of a vertical line is undefined.
explanation: Linear equations of the form ax + by + c = 0 represent straight lines.
The slope measures the steepness of a line and is calculated using two points.
Horizontal lines have no incline, and vertical lines have an undefined slope.

flashcards.title: Properties of Straight Lines
formulas: Two lines are parallel if their slopes are equal.
Two lines are perpendicular if the product of their slopes is -1.
Three points P, Q, and R are collinear if the slope of PQ = slope of QR.
explanation: Parallel lines have the same slope and never intersect.
Perpendicular lines form a 90° angle, and their slopes multiply to -1.
Collinear points lie on the same line, verified using their slopes.

flashcards.title: Forms of Equation of a Line
formulas: Slope-intercept form: y = mx + c, where m is the slope and c is the y-intercept.
Point-slope form: y - y₁ = m(x - x₁), where m is the slope, and (x₁, y₁) is a point on the line.
Two-point form: y - y₁ = [(y₂ - y₁) / (x₂ - x₁)](x - x₁).
Intercept form: x/a + y/b = 1, where a and b are the x- and y-intercepts.
explanation: The slope-intercept form gives a direct relationship between x and y.
The point-slope form is used when a point and slope are known.
The two-point form calculates the equation from two given points.
The intercept form uses the x- and y-intercepts to describe the line.

flashcards.title: Special Cases and Conditions
formulas: Equation of x-axis: y = 0.
Equation of y-axis: x = 0.
Equation of a line parallel to the x-axis: y = a.
Equation of a line parallel to the y-axis: x = b.
explanation: The x-axis is a horizontal line where y = 0.
The y-axis is a vertical line where x = 0.
A line parallel to the x-axis is horizontal at a fixed y-value.
A line parallel to the y-axis is vertical at a fixed x-value.

flashcards.title: Perpendicular Distance from a Point
formulas: Distance of a point (x₁, y₁) from a line ax + by + c = 0 is d = |ax₁ + by₁ + c| / √(a² + b²).
Distance between parallel lines ax + by + c₁ = 0 and ax + by + c₂ = 0 is d = |c₂ - c₁| / √(a² + b²).
explanation: The perpendicular distance formula gives the shortest distance from a point to a line.
The distance between two parallel lines is constant and uses their difference in constants.

flashcards.title: Angle Between Two Lines
formulas: tan θ = |(m₂ - m₁) / (1 + m₁m₂)|, where m₁ and m₂ are the slopes of the two lines.
explanation: The angle between two lines depends on their slopes and is calculated using this formula.

flashcards.title: Basics of Conic Sections
formulas: A conic section is the intersection of a plane with a double-napped cone.
The different types of conic sections are: Circle, Parabola, Ellipse, and Hyperbola.
General equation of a conic section: Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0.
explanation: Conic sections are obtained by cutting a cone at different angles.
The type of conic depends on the angle between the plane and the cone.
The general equation represents all conic sections, determined by the coefficients.

flashcards.title: Circle
formulas: Standard equation of a circle: (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r².
Equation of a circle centered at the origin: x² + y² = r².
General equation of a circle: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0.
explanation: The standard form represents a circle with a center (h, k) and radius r.
If the center is at the origin, the equation simplifies to this form.
The general form can be converted into standard form to find center and radius.

flashcards.title: Parabola
formulas: Standard equation of a parabola: y² = 4ax (opens right), x² = 4ay (opens up).
Vertex: (0, 0); Focus: (a, 0) for y² = 4ax; (0, a) for x² = 4ay.
Equation of directrix: x = -a for y² = 4ax; y = -a for x² = 4ay.
explanation: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from the focus and directrix.
The vertex is the point of intersection of the axis of symmetry and parabola.
The directrix is a line perpendicular to the axis of symmetry.

flashcards.title: Ellipse
formulas: Standard equation of an ellipse: (x²/a²) + (y²/b²) = 1 (horizontal major axis).
Foci: (±c, 0), where c² = a² - b² for horizontal major axis.
Eccentricity: e = c/a, where 0 < e < 1.
explanation: An ellipse is the set of points where the sum of distances from the foci is constant.
The foci are the fixed points that define the shape of the ellipse.
The eccentricity measures the deviation of the ellipse from being a circle.

flashcards.title: Hyperbola
formulas: Standard equation of a hyperbola: (x²/a²) - (y²/b²) = 1 (horizontal transverse axis).
Foci: (±c, 0), where c² = a² + b² for horizontal transverse axis.
Eccentricity: e = c/a, where e > 1.
explanation: A hyperbola is the set of points where the absolute difference of distances from the foci is constant.
The foci are fixed points that define the hyperbola, located further apart than in an ellipse.
The eccentricity of a hyperbola is always greater than 1, defining its open shape.

flashcards.title: Special Properties of Conics
formulas: Focus-Directrix Property: e = distance from focus / distance from directrix.
For all conics, e = 1 (parabola), e < 1 (ellipse), e > 1 (hyperbola).
Reflection Property: Light or sound from one focus reflects to the other focus.
explanation: This property relates the shape of the conic section to its eccentricity.
The eccentricity classifies the conic as a parabola, ellipse, or hyperbola.
The reflection property is unique to ellipses and hyperbolas.

flashcards.title: Basics of 3D Geometry
formulas: In 3D, the coordinate axes are three mutually perpendicular lines: x, y, and z axes.
The coordinate planes are: xy-plane, yz-plane, and zx-plane.
The coordinates of a point P in 3D space are written as (x, y, z).
explanation: The three axes divide the space into eight regions called octants.
Each coordinate plane is formed by a pair of axes and divides the space further.
The coordinates of a point represent its perpendicular distances from the coordinate planes.

flashcards.title: Point Representation
formulas: Points on x-axis are of the form (x, 0, 0).
Points on y-axis are of the form (0, y, 0).
Points on z-axis are of the form (0, 0, z).
explanation: Points on the x-axis have zero y and z coordinates.
Points on the y-axis have zero x and z coordinates.
Points on the z-axis have zero x and y coordinates.

flashcards.title: Distance Formula
formulas: Distance between two points P(x₁, y₁, z₁) and Q(x₂, y₂, z₂):
PQ = √[(x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)² + (z₂ - z₁)²]
explanation: The distance formula calculates the straight-line distance between two points.
It extends the 2D distance formula by including the z-coordinate differences.

flashcards.title: Division of Line Segment
formulas: Coordinates of R dividing a line internally: R = [(mx₂ + nx₁) / (m + n), (my₂ + ny₁) / (m + n), (mz₂ + nz₁) / (m + n)].
Coordinates of R dividing a line externally: R = [(mx₂ - nx₁) / (m - n), (my₂ - ny₁) / (m - n), (mz₂ - nz₁) / (m - n)].
explanation: The internal division formula calculates a point dividing the line in a specific ratio inside the segment.
The external division formula calculates a point dividing the line externally in a given ratio.

flashcards.title: Midpoint and Centroid
formulas: Midpoint: M = [(x₁ + x₂) / 2, (y₁ + y₂) / 2, (z₁ + z₂) / 2].
Centroid: G = [(x₁ + x₂ + x₃) / 3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃) / 3, (z₁ + z₂ + z₃) / 3].
explanation: The midpoint formula finds the point exactly halfway between two points.
The centroid formula gives the center of mass of a triangle, assuming uniform density.

flashcards.title: Distance from Origin
formulas: Distance of a point P(x, y, z) from the origin O(0, 0, 0):
OP = √(x² + y² + z²)
explanation: This formula calculates the straight-line distance from the origin to the point.
It is derived from the Pythagorean theorem in three dimensions.

flashcards.title: Definition of Limits
formulas: lim f(x) as x → a = L if lim f(x) from left = lim f(x) from right = L
lim (f(x) ± g(x)) = lim f(x) ± lim g(x)
lim (f(x) * g(x)) = lim f(x) * lim g(x)
lim (f(x) / g(x)) = lim f(x) / lim g(x), provided lim g(x) ≠ 0
explanation: The limit of a function exists if the left-hand limit and right-hand limit are equal.
The sum or difference of limits is the limit of their sum or difference.
The product of limits is the limit of their product.
The quotient of limits is the limit of their quotient, provided the denominator is non-zero.

flashcards.title: Special Limits
formulas: lim (1 + x)^(1/x) as x → 0 = e
lim sin(x) / x as x → 0 = 1
lim (1 - cos(x)) / x² as x → 0 = 1/2
lim log(1 + x) / x as x → 0 = 1
explanation: This is a fundamental limit defining the constant 'e'.
The ratio of sin(x) to x approaches 1 as x tends to 0.
The limit of (1 - cos(x)) divided by x² as x approaches 0 is 1/2.
The logarithmic limit as x approaches 0 is 1.

flashcards.title: Definition of Derivatives
formulas: dy/dx = lim (Δx → 0) [Δy / Δx]
explanation: The derivative of a function is the limit of the average rate of change as the interval approaches 0.
The derivative dy/dx represents the instantaneous rate of change of y with respect to x.

flashcards.title: Standard Derivatives
formulas: d/dx (xⁿ) = n * x^(n-1)
d/dx (e^x) = e^x
d/dx (sin(x)) = cos(x)
d/dx (log(x)) = 1/x
explanation: The derivative of xⁿ is n times x raised to the power of (n-1).
The derivative of the exponential function is itself.
The derivative of sin(x) is cos(x).
The derivative of log(x) is 1 divided by x.

flashcards.title: Rules of Differentiation
formulas: d/dx [f(x) + g(x)] = f'(x) + g'(x)
d/dx [f(x) * g(x)] = f(x)g'(x) + g(x)f'(x)
d/dx [f(x) / g(x)] = [g(x)f'(x) - f(x)g'(x)] / [g(x)]²
explanation: The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives.
The product rule states that the derivative of a product is given by this formula.
The quotient rule gives the derivative of the division of two functions.

flashcards.title: Applications of Derivatives
formulas: Slope of tangent = dy/dx
Rate of change = dy/dx
explanation: The derivative represents the slope of the tangent line at a point on the curve.
The derivative also gives the instantaneous rate of change of a quantity.

flashcards.title: Basic Concepts of Statements
explanation: A statement is a mathematically acceptable sentence that is either true or false but not both.
The negation of a statement p is denoted by ~p and is read as 'not p'.
A compound statement is made up of two or more simple statements connected by words like 'and', 'or', 'if-then', etc.

flashcards.title: Compound Statements with 'AND'
explanation: The compound statement with 'AND' is true if all its component statements are true.
It is false if any one of its component statements is false.

flashcards.title: Compound Statements with 'OR'
explanation: The compound statement with 'OR' is true when at least one of its component statements is true.
It is false only when all its component statements are false.

flashcards.title: Conditional Statements
explanation: A sentence with 'If p, then q' can be written as:
i) p implies q (denoted by p → q).
ii) p is a sufficient condition for q.
iii) q is a necessary condition for p.
iv) q only if p.

flashcards.title: Contrapositive, Converse, and Inverse
explanation: The contrapositive of p → q is q → ~p.
The converse of p → q is q → p.
The inverse of p → q is ~p → ~q.

flashcards.title: Quantifiers
explanation: The term 'for all' is called a universal quantifier.
The term 'there exists' is called an existential quantifier.

flashcards.title: Validity of Statements
explanation: A statement is valid if it is true in all cases.
A statement is invalid if it is false in any case.

flashcards.title: Logical Equivalences
explanation: The statement 'p and q' is true if both p and q are true.
The statement 'p or q' is true if at least one of p or q is true.
The statement 'if p, then q' is true in all cases except when p is true and q is false.

flashcards.title: Measures of Dispersion
explanation: Dispersion measures the scatteredness around the central value.
Measures of dispersion include Range, Quartile deviation, Mean deviation, and Standard deviation.
Range is the difference between the greatest and least values of the variable.

flashcards.title: Mean Deviation for Individual Observations
formulas: M.D. = (1/n) Σ|xᵢ - a|, where a = mean, median, or mode.
M.D. = a + h * (1/n) Σ|uᵢ|, where uᵢ = (xᵢ - a)/h
explanation: Mean deviation is the average of the absolute deviations from a chosen central value (mean, median, or mode).
The formula accounts for deviations scaled by a factor h.

flashcards.title: Mean Deviation for Discrete Frequency Distribution
formulas: M.D. = (1/N) Σfᵢ|xᵢ - a|, where a = mean, median, or mode.
M.D. = a + h * (1/N) Σfᵢ|uᵢ|, where uᵢ = (xᵢ - a)/h
explanation: Mean deviation for grouped data considers the frequency of each observation.
The deviations are scaled and weighted by their frequencies.

flashcards.title: Standard Deviation
formulas: σ = √Variance
explanation: Standard deviation is the square root of the variance and measures the spread of data points.

flashcards.title: Variance for Individual Observations
formulas: Variance(X) = (1/n) Σ(xᵢ - X̄)²
Var(X) = h² * [(1/n) Σuᵢ² - ((1/n) Σuᵢ)²], where uᵢ = (xᵢ - a)/h
explanation: Variance is the arithmetic mean of squared deviations from the mean.
The formula with scaling factor h accounts for deviations in standardized units.

flashcards.title: Variance for Discrete Frequency Distribution
formulas: Variance(X) = (1/N) Σfᵢ(xᵢ - X̄)²
Var(X) = h² * [(1/N) Σfᵢuᵢ² - ((1/N) Σfᵢuᵢ)²], where uᵢ = (xᵢ - a)/h
explanation: Variance for grouped data considers the frequency of each observation.
The formula accounts for frequency-weighted squared deviations from the mean.

flashcards.title: Coefficient of Variation
explanation: The coefficient of variation compares the variability of two or more frequency distributions.
A higher coefficient of variation indicates greater variability around the central value.

flashcards.title: Basic Concepts of Probability
explanation: An experiment whose outcomes cannot be predicted in advance is called a random experiment.
Each outcome of a random experiment is called an elementary event.
The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment is called the sample space.

flashcards.title: Types of Events
explanation: An event is a subset of the sample space.
A certain event always occurs in an experiment, while an impossible event never occurs.
Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur simultaneously.

flashcards.title: Probability Axioms
formulas: 0 ≤ P(ω) ≤ 1 for all ω ∈ S
P(A) = Σ P(ω) for ω ∈ A
explanation: The probability of any event lies between 0 and 1.
The probability of the entire sample space is 1.
The probability of an event is the sum of probabilities of its elementary events.

flashcards.title: Classical Definition of Probability
formulas: P(A) = m / n
explanation: Probability is the ratio of favorable outcomes to the total number of outcomes in the sample space.

flashcards.title: Addition Rule of Probability
formulas: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B)
If A and B are mutually exclusive, then P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B)
explanation: The probability of union of two events is the sum of their probabilities minus the probability of their intersection.
For mutually exclusive events, the intersection probability is zero.

flashcards.title: Probability for Three Events
formulas: P(A ∪ B ∪ C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(A ∩ B) - P(B ∩ C) - P(C ∩ A) + P(A ∩ B ∩ C)
explanation: The probability of union of three events includes all individual probabilities, subtracts pairwise intersections, and adds the triple intersection.

flashcards.title: Special Cases for Two Events
formulas: P(A ∩ B') = P(A) - P(A ∩ B)
P(A' ∩ B) = P(B) - P(A ∩ B)
P(A ∪ B) - P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) - 2P(A ∩ B)
explanation: The probability of A and not B is the probability of A minus their intersection.
The probability of not A and B is the probability of B minus their intersection.
The probability of exactly one of A or B is calculated using this formula.

flashcards.title: Basic Concepts of Relations
formulas: A relation R from A to B is a subset of A × B.
Domain of R: {a ∈ A | (a, b) ∈ R for some b ∈ B}.
Range of R: {b ∈ B | (a, b) ∈ R for some a ∈ A}.
explanation: A relation is a subset of the Cartesian product of two sets.
The domain of a relation is the set of all first elements in the ordered pairs.
The range of a relation is the set of all second elements in the ordered pairs.

flashcards.title: Inverse and Composition of Relations
formulas: Inverse relation: R⁻¹ = {(b, a) | (a, b) ∈ R}.
Composition of relations R and S: SoR = {(a, c) | (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ S}.
explanation: The inverse of a relation swaps the elements in each pair.
The composition of two relations creates a new relation linking the first set of one relation to the second set of the other.

flashcards.title: Properties of Relations
formulas: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for all a ∈ A.
Symmetric: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R.
Transitive: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R.
explanation: A relation is reflexive if every element is related to itself.
A relation is symmetric if reversing the pair does not affect membership.
A relation is transitive if chaining relations results in a new relation.

flashcards.title: Functions and Their Types
formulas: A function f: A → B maps each element of A to a unique element of B.
One-to-One (Injective): f(a₁) = f(a₂) ⇒ a₁ = a₂.
Onto (Surjective): Range(f) = Codomain(f).
Bijective: A function is both injective and surjective.
explanation: A function maps elements from one set to another with unique assignments.
Injective functions have distinct outputs for distinct inputs.
Surjective functions cover the entire codomain.
Bijective functions are both one-to-one and onto.

flashcards.title: Special Functions
formulas: Identity function: Iₐ(x) = x for all x ∈ A.
Constant function: f(a) = c for all a ∈ A.
Inverse function: f⁻¹(b) = a ⇔ f(a) = b.
Composite function: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).
explanation: The identity function maps each element to itself.
A constant function assigns the same value to all inputs.
An inverse function reverses the mapping of the original function.
The composite function combines two functions into one.

flashcards.title: Binary Operations
formulas: A binary operation * on a set A satisfies: *: A × A → A.
Commutative: a * b = b * a for all a, b ∈ A.
Associative: (a * b) * c = a * (b * c) for all a, b, c ∈ A.
Identity element e: a * e = e * a = a for all a ∈ A.
explanation: Binary operations combine two elements from a set to produce another element of the same set.
Commutative operations have the same result regardless of the order of elements.
Associative operations group elements without changing the result.
An identity element leaves other elements unchanged when combined.

flashcards.title: Connecting Concepts
formulas: f: A → B and g: B → C ⇒ g ∘ f: A → C.
Number of injections from A to B: P(m, n) = m! / (m - n)! (if |A| = n, |B| = m).
explanation: Composition of functions links multiple mappings into one.
The number of injective functions depends on the sizes of the sets.

flashcards.title: Domains and Ranges of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
formulas: sin⁻¹(x): Domain = [-1, 1], Range = [-π/2, π/2]
cos⁻¹(x): Domain = [-1, 1], Range = [0, π]
tan⁻¹(x): Domain = R, Range = (-π/2, π/2)
cosec⁻¹(x): Domain = R \ [-1, 1], Range = [-π/2, 0) ∪ (0, π/2]
sec⁻¹(x): Domain = R \ [-1, 1], Range = [0, π] \ {π/2}
cot⁻¹(x): Domain = R, Range = (0, π)
explanation: Inverse trigonometric functions have specific domains and ranges to ensure they are one-to-one.
The domain of sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹ is restricted to [-1, 1] because sine and cosine values are in this range.
Other functions like tan⁻¹ and cot⁻¹ are defined over all real numbers.

flashcards.title: Principal Value Branches
formulas: sin⁻¹(x): Principal value = [-π/2, π/2]
cos⁻¹(x): Principal value = [0, π]
tan⁻¹(x): Principal value = [-π/2, π/2]
cosec⁻¹(x): Principal value = [-π/2, π/2] \ {0}
sec⁻¹(x): Principal value = [0, π] \ {π/2}
cot⁻¹(x): Principal value = (0, π)
explanation: Principal value branches define unique values for inverse trigonometric functions within a specified range.
For example, the principal value of sin⁻¹(x) lies in [-π/2, π/2], ensuring a unique output for each input.

flashcards.title: Graphs of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
explanation: The graph of sin⁻¹(x) is a reflection of y = sin(x) across the line y = x.
Similarly, cos⁻¹(x), tan⁻¹(x), and other functions are obtained by reflecting their respective trigonometric functions.

flashcards.title: Connecting Concepts
formulas: sin⁻¹(x) + cos⁻¹(x) = π/2
tan⁻¹(x) + cot⁻¹(x) = π/2
sec⁻¹(x) + cosec⁻¹(x) = π/2
2cos⁻¹(x) = cos⁻¹(2x²-1), |x| ≤ 1
explanation: These identities relate pairs of inverse trigonometric functions.
For example, sin⁻¹(x) + cos⁻¹(x) always equals π/2, showing their complementary nature.
Other formulas express double angles and transformations in terms of inverse functions.

flashcards.title: Introduction to Matrices
formulas: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns.
Order of a matrix: If a matrix has m rows and n columns, its order is m × n.
A square matrix has an equal number of rows and columns.
A null matrix has all its elements equal to zero.
explanation: Matrices are used to represent systems of linear equations and transformations.
The order specifies the dimensions of the matrix.
Square matrices are symmetric about their diagonal.
The null matrix represents a matrix with no values other than zero.

flashcards.title: Special Types of Matrices
formulas: Diagonal Matrix: A matrix with non-zero elements only on its diagonal.
Scalar Matrix: A diagonal matrix where all diagonal elements are equal.
Unit Matrix (Identity Matrix): A square matrix with diagonal elements equal to 1.
Upper Triangular Matrix: A matrix where all elements below the diagonal are zero.
Lower Triangular Matrix: A matrix where all elements above the diagonal are zero.
explanation: Diagonal matrices simplify operations as only diagonal elements are non-zero.
Scalar matrices are a subset of diagonal matrices with uniform diagonal values.
Identity matrices act as the multiplicative identity in matrix operations.
Upper and lower triangular matrices have zero elements either above or below the diagonal.

flashcards.title: Matrix Operations
formulas: Addition: If A and B are matrices of the same order, then A + B = [aᵢⱼ + bᵢⱼ].
Scalar Multiplication: If K is a scalar, then K × A = [k × aᵢⱼ].
Matrix Multiplication: If A is m × n and B is n × p, then AB is m × p.
Transpose of a Matrix: If A is a matrix, then Aᵀ = [aⱼᵢ].
explanation: Matrix addition is performed element-wise, requiring matrices to have the same order.
Scalar multiplication scales every element of the matrix by a constant.
Matrix multiplication combines rows of A with columns of B.
The transpose of a matrix swaps its rows with columns.

flashcards.title: Properties of Matrices
formulas: Commutative Property of Addition: A + B = B + A.
Associative Property of Addition: (A + B) + C = A + (B + C).
Distributive Property: K(A + B) = KA + KB.
Associative Property of Multiplication: (AB)C = A(BC).
Transpose Properties: (A + B)ᵀ = Aᵀ + Bᵀ and (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ.
explanation: Addition of matrices is commutative and associative.
Distributive property holds for both scalar multiplication and matrix addition.
Matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative.
Transpose operation reverses the order in multiplication.

flashcards.title: Determinants and Inverse of Matrices
formulas: Determinant of a 2x2 Matrix: |A| = ad - bc for A = [[a, b], [c, d]].
A matrix is invertible if |A| ≠ 0.
Inverse of a Matrix: A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) * adj(A), where adj(A) is the adjoint of A.
explanation: The determinant provides a scalar value representing the matrix's scale factor.
A matrix is invertible only if its determinant is non-zero.
The inverse of a matrix is used to solve systems of linear equations.

flashcards.title: Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices
formulas: Symmetric Matrix: A matrix A is symmetric if A = Aᵀ.
Skew-Symmetric Matrix: A matrix A is skew-symmetric if Aᵀ = -A.
explanation: Symmetric matrices are equal to their transpose.
Skew-symmetric matrices are the negation of their transpose.

flashcards.title: Basics of Determinants
formulas: |A| = a11 * a22 - a12 * a21 (for 2x2 matrix)
|A| = Σ(ai1 * Ci1), where Ci1 is the cofactor of ai1 (general determinant formula)
explanation: A determinant represents a specific type of numerical value associated with a square matrix.
The value of a determinant for a 2x2 matrix is computed as the product of its diagonals minus the product of its off-diagonals.
For larger matrices, determinants are expanded using cofactors.

flashcards.title: Minors and Cofactors
formulas: Minor Mij = determinant of the matrix obtained by deleting the i-th row and j-th column.
Cofactor Cij = (-1)^(i+j) * Mij
explanation: The minor of an element is the determinant of the smaller matrix left after removing the element's row and column.
The cofactor is the signed version of the minor, depending on the position of the element in the matrix.

flashcards.title: Area of a Triangle Using Determinants
explanation: The determinant can be used to calculate the area of a triangle given its vertices.
The formula involves placing the vertices in a determinant, computing its absolute value, and dividing by 2.

flashcards.title: System of Linear Equations
formulas: AX = B
X = A^(-1) * B (if A is invertible)
explanation: A system of linear equations can be expressed as a matrix equation.
If the determinant of the coefficient matrix (A) is non-zero, the system has a unique solution.

flashcards.title: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
formulas: Adj(A) = transpose of cofactor matrix of A
explanation: The adjoint of a matrix is obtained by taking the transpose of its cofactor matrix.
The inverse of a matrix exists only if its determinant is non-zero and is computed using the adjoint.

flashcards.title: Properties of Determinants
formulas: Interchanging two rows: |A| changes sign.
Multiplying a row by k: |A| is multiplied by k.
|A| = 0 if two rows (or columns) are identical or proportional.
explanation: Interchanging two rows or columns in a determinant reverses its sign.
Scaling a row or column scales the determinant by the same factor.
If any two rows or columns are identical, the determinant is zero.

flashcards.title: Special Determinant Rules
formulas: |kA| = k^n * |A| (for an n x n matrix)
explanation: Scaling the entire matrix by a constant scales the determinant by the constant raised to the power of the matrix's order.
The determinant of the product of two matrices is the product of their determinants.

flashcards.title: Connecting Concepts
formulas: If |A| = 0, the matrix is singular.
If A is invertible, |A| ≠ 0.
explanation: A determinant of zero indicates a singular matrix, which does not have an inverse.
The invertibility of a matrix is directly linked to its determinant being non-zero.

flashcards.title: Continuity
formulas: lim f(x) as x → a = f(a)
lim f(a+h) as h → 0 = lim f(a-h) = f(a)
explanation: A function is continuous at x = a if the limit of the function exists, is finite, and equals the function's value at a.
Continuity in an interval means the function is continuous at each point of the interval.

flashcards.title: Discontinuity
explanation: A function is discontinuous at x = a if it is not continuous at this point.
Discontinuity occurs where the limit of the function does not exist, is not finite, or does not equal the function value.

flashcards.title: Differentiability
formulas: f'(x) = lim h → 0 [(f(x+h) - f(x)) / h]
explanation: Differentiability means the derivative of the function exists at a given point.
Every differentiable function is continuous, but not every continuous function is differentiable.

flashcards.title: Algebra of Derivatives
formulas: (uv)' = u'v + uv'
(u/v)' = (u'v - uv') / v²
explanation: The sum, product, and quotient of differentiable functions follow specific rules for derivatives.
The quotient rule requires that the denominator is not zero.

flashcards.title: Chain Rule
explanation: The chain rule is used to differentiate composite functions.
If y = f(u) and u = g(x), then dy/dx = (dy/du) * (du/dx).

flashcards.title: Implicit Differentiation
formulas: Differentiate both sides of the equation term-wise with respect to x.
Collect terms containing dy/dx to isolate and solve for dy/dx.
explanation: Implicit differentiation is used when y is not explicitly expressed as a function of x.
Each occurrence of y is differentiated with respect to x, multiplying by dy/dx.

flashcards.title: Logarithmic Differentiation
formulas: log_b(pq) = log_b(p) + log_b(q)
log_b(p/q) = log_b(p) - log_b(q)
log_b(p^x) = x * log_b(p)
explanation: Logarithmic differentiation simplifies the differentiation of functions with exponents or products.
It involves taking the natural logarithm of both sides of the function.

flashcards.title: Derivatives of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
formulas: d/dx [sin⁻¹(x)] = 1 / √(1-x²)
d/dx [cos⁻¹(x)] = -1 / √(1-x²)
d/dx [tan⁻¹(x)] = 1 / (1+x²)
d/dx [cot⁻¹(x)] = -1 / (1+x²)
d/dx [sec⁻¹(x)] = 1 / |x|√(x²-1)
d/dx [cosec⁻¹(x)] = -1 / |x|√(x²-1)
explanation: These formulas provide the derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions.
They are used in calculus to compute the slopes of curves defined by such functions.

flashcards.title: Mean Value Theorem
explanation: For a function continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), there exists a point c in (a, b) where the tangent is parallel to the secant joining (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)).

flashcards.title: Rolle's Theorem
explanation: If f(a) = f(b) and the function is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), there exists a c in (a, b) such that f'(c) = 0.

flashcards.title: Rate of Change and Increasing/Decreasing Functions
formulas: dy/dx = lim Δx→0 [Δy/Δx]
f'(x0) represents the rate of change of y with respect to x at x = x0
f'(x) > 0 for increasing functions
f'(x) < 0 for decreasing functions
explanation: Rate of change indicates how one quantity changes with respect to another.
A function is increasing if f'(x) > 0 and decreasing if f'(x) < 0 in a given interval.

flashcards.title: Tangents, Normals, and Extrema
formulas: Tangent: y - y0 = m(x - x0), where m = f'(x0)
Normal: y - y0 = (-1/m)(x - x0), where m = f'(x0)
Maximum: f'(x) = 0 and f''(x) < 0
Minimum: f'(x) = 0 and f''(x) > 0
explanation: The tangent to a curve at a point has a slope equal to the derivative at that point.
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent.
A maximum occurs when f'(x) = 0 and f''(x) < 0, while a minimum occurs when f'(x) = 0 and f''(x) > 0.

flashcards.title: Local and Absolute Extrema
formulas: Absolute extrema: Consider critical points and endpoints.
Local extrema: f'(c) = 0, and f''(c) determines the nature of the point.
explanation: Absolute extrema occur over the entire interval, while local extrema occur within a smaller neighborhood.
The first derivative test can identify the nature of local extrema by observing the sign changes in f'(x).

flashcards.title: Connecting Concepts: Increasing/Decreasing and Tangents
formulas: Increasing: If x1 < x2, then f(x1) ≤ f(x2).
Strictly Increasing: If x1 < x2, then f(x1) < f(x2).
Decreasing: If x1 < x2, then f(x1) ≥ f(x2).
Strictly Decreasing: If x1 < x2, then f(x1) > f(x2).
Tangent special cases: If θ = 0, m = 0 → y = y0; If θ = π/2, m is undefined → x = x0
explanation: An increasing function rises as x increases, while a decreasing function falls.
The tangent's slope depends on m, derived from the angle θ with respect to the x-axis.

flashcards.title: Introduction to Integration
formulas: ∫ f'(x) dx = f(x) + C
d/dx [F(x) + C] = f(x)
explanation: Integration is the process of finding the function F(x) whose derivative is f(x).
The arbitrary constant C is added because the integral of a function is not unique.

flashcards.title: Integration by Substitution
formulas: Let x = g(t), dx = g'(t) dt
∫ f(x) dx = ∫ f(g(t)) g'(t) dt
explanation: Use substitution when the integrand can be simplified by expressing it in terms of another variable.
Common substitutions: x = a sin(θ), x = a tan(θ), x = a sec(θ).

flashcards.title: Trigonometric Integrals
formulas: ∫ sin(ax) cos(bx) dx = (1/2) ∫ [sin((a+b)x) + sin((a-b)x)] dx
explanation: Trigonometric products are often expressed as sums or differences using identities.
This helps simplify integration involving sin(x), cos(x), and their powers.

flashcards.title: Integration of Rational Functions
formulas: ∫ P(x)/Q(x) dx = ∫ [T(x) + P1(x)/Q1(x)] dx
Where T(x) is the quotient and P1(x)/Q1(x) is the proper rational fraction.
explanation: For rational functions, use polynomial long division if the numerator's degree is greater than or equal to the denominator's.
Decompose proper fractions into partial fractions for easier integration.

flashcards.title: Integration by Parts
formulas: ∫ u v dx = u ∫ v dx - ∫ (du/dx) ∫ v dx
explanation: Use integration by parts when the integrand is a product of two functions.
Choose u and dv based on ILATE (Inverse, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential) rule.

flashcards.title: Definite Integrals
formulas: ∫[a to b] f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)
∫[a to b] f(x) dx = ∫[a to b] f(a+b-x) dx
explanation: Definite integrals provide the net area under the curve of f(x) between limits a and b.
Properties like symmetry and substitution simplify evaluation of definite integrals.

flashcards.title: General Properties of Integrals
formulas: ∫ k f(x) dx = k ∫ f(x) dx
∫[a to b] f(x) dx = -∫[b to a] f(x) dx
∫[a to b] [f(x) + g(x)] dx = ∫[a to b] f(x) dx + ∫[a to b] g(x) dx
explanation: Integration is linear and follows basic algebraic rules.
Reversal of limits changes the sign of the integral.

flashcards.title: Special Integrals
formulas: ∫ dx / (x^2 + a^2) = (1/a) arctan(x/a) + C
∫ dx / sqrt(x^2 + a^2) = log|x + sqrt(x^2 + a^2)| + C
explanation: These are standard results for common forms of integrals.
These results are derived from trigonometric or logarithmic substitutions.

flashcards.title: Area Under Simple Curves
formulas: A = ∫[a to b] f(x) dx
explanation: The area under the curve y = f(x), bounded by the x-axis and the vertical lines x = a and x = b, is calculated as the definite integral of f(x) from a to b.
The integral represents the sum of the areas of thin vertical strips under the curve.

flashcards.title: Area Between Two Curves
formulas: A = ∫[a to b] [f(x) - g(x)] dx
explanation: The area between two curves y = f(x) and y = g(x), where f(x) > g(x) over [a, b], is the integral of the difference between the two functions from a to b.
If the roles of f(x) and g(x) interchange, the formula remains the same as it calculates the absolute difference.

flashcards.title: Area for Curves Below the X-Axis
formulas: A = ∫[a to b] |f(x)| dx
explanation: If the curve lies below the x-axis, f(x) < 0, and the integral gives a negative value. In such cases, the absolute value of the integral represents the area.

flashcards.title: Area for Curves Partly Above and Below the X-Axis
formulas: A = |∫[a to c] f(x) dx| + |∫[c to b] f(x) dx|
explanation: If a portion of the curve is above the x-axis and a portion is below, the total area is the sum of the absolute values of the integrals over the respective intervals.

flashcards.title: General Case for Area Between Two Curves
formulas: A = ∫[a to c] [f(x) - g(x)] dx + ∫[c to b] [g(x) - f(x)] dx
explanation: For two curves intersecting at points a, c, and b, the area is calculated by dividing the interval [a, b] at the intersection points and integrating the difference accordingly.

flashcards.title: Basic Concepts of Differential Equations
explanation: A differential equation involves an independent variable, a dependent variable, and derivatives of the dependent variable with respect to the independent variable.
Order: The order of a differential equation is the highest order derivative present in the equation.
Degree: The degree of a differential equation is the power of the highest order derivative, provided it is free from radicals or fractions.

flashcards.title: Solution of a Differential Equation
explanation: General Solution: Contains arbitrary constants equal to the order of the equation.
Particular Solution: Obtained by assigning specific values to the arbitrary constants in the general solution.

flashcards.title: Variable Separable Form
formulas: dy/dx = f(x)g(y) → ∫(1/g(y)) dy = ∫f(x) dx
explanation: If the equation can be written such that all terms involving y are on one side and all terms involving x are on the other, the variables are separable.
The solution is obtained by integrating both sides.

flashcards.title: Homogeneous Differential Equations
formulas: dy/dx = F(x, y) where F(kx, ky) = F(x, y)
explanation: A differential equation is homogeneous if it can be expressed as a function of the ratio y/x.
To solve, substitute y = vx (or x = vy) and separate the variables.

flashcards.title: Linear Differential Equations
formulas: dy/dx + Py = Q
Integrating factor (I.F.) = e^(∫P dx)
Solution: y * I.F. = ∫(Q * I.F.) dx + C
explanation: A linear differential equation has the form dy/dx + Py = Q, where P and Q are functions of x.
The solution involves finding the integrating factor and integrating accordingly.

flashcards.title: Formation of Differential Equations
explanation: Differential equations can be formed by differentiating an equation containing arbitrary constants.
Eliminate the arbitrary constants to obtain the differential equation.

flashcards.title: Basic Concepts of Vectors
explanation: A vector is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, force, or acceleration.
The magnitude of a vector is the distance between its initial and terminal points.
Vectors are denoted using bold letters or arrows above the symbol (e.g., AB or →AB).

flashcards.title: Types of Vectors
explanation: Zero Vector: A vector with both initial and terminal points coinciding.
Unit Vector: A vector with magnitude equal to 1, denoted as û.
Co-initial Vectors: Vectors having the same initial point.
Collinear Vectors: Vectors parallel to the same line.
Equal Vectors: Vectors with the same magnitude and direction.
Negative Vector: A vector with the same magnitude but opposite direction.

flashcards.title: Addition of Vectors
formulas: a + b = resultant vector using triangle or parallelogram law.
explanation: The sum of two vectors is found by placing them head-to-tail and joining the initial point of the first vector to the terminal point of the second.
The parallelogram law states that the resultant of two vectors is represented by the diagonal of a parallelogram.

flashcards.title: Multiplication of a Vector by a Scalar
formulas: λa = scalar multiple of vector a
explanation: When a vector is multiplied by a scalar, its magnitude changes but its direction remains the same.
If λ is negative, the vector's direction is reversed.

flashcards.title: Components of a Vector
formulas: a = xi + yj + zk
|a| = √(x² + y² + z²)
explanation: A vector in three-dimensional space can be expressed in terms of its components along the x, y, and z axes.
The unit vectors along the axes are i, j, and k, respectively.

flashcards.title: Section Formula
formulas: r = (mb + na) / (m + n) for internal division
r = (mb - na) / (m - n) for external division
explanation: The section formula gives the position vector of a point dividing a line segment in a given ratio.

flashcards.title: Dot Product of Two Vectors
formulas: a · b = |a||b|cos(θ)
explanation: The dot product is a scalar quantity representing the projection of one vector onto another.
If θ = 90°, then a · b = 0 (vectors are perpendicular).

flashcards.title: Cross Product of Two Vectors
formulas: a × b = |a||b|sin(θ)n̂
explanation: The cross product is a vector perpendicular to both a and b.
If θ = 0° or 180°, then a × b = 0 (vectors are parallel).

flashcards.title: Distance Formula
explanation: The distance between two points A(x1, y1, z1) and B(x2, y2, z2) in three-dimensional space is calculated using the distance formula.

flashcards.title: Section Formula
formulas: R = (mx2 + nx1) / (m + n), (my2 + ny1) / (m + n), (mz2 + nz1) / (m + n) (Internal Division)
R = (mx2 - nx1) / (m - n), (my2 - ny1) / (m - n), (mz2 - nz1) / (m - n) (External Division)
explanation: The section formula determines the coordinates of a point dividing a line segment in a given ratio m:n, either internally or externally.

flashcards.title: Mid-Point Formula
explanation: The midpoint formula calculates the point that divides a line segment into two equal parts.

flashcards.title: Centroid Formula
explanation: The centroid of a triangle in three-dimensional space is the average of the coordinates of its vertices.

flashcards.title: Position in Three-Dimensional Space
explanation: A rectangular coordinate system consists of three mutually perpendicular axes: x, y, and z.
The three planes formed by these axes are called the coordinate planes: XY-plane, YZ-plane, and ZX-plane.
The coordinates (x, y, z) of a point are its perpendicular distances from the YZ, ZX, and XY planes, respectively.

flashcards.title: Distance of a Point from the Origin
formulas: Distance = √(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)
explanation: The distance of a point (x, y, z) from the origin (0, 0, 0) is calculated using the Pythagorean theorem in three dimensions.

flashcards.title: Octants and Coordinate Signs
explanation: The space is divided into 8 parts called octants based on the signs of the x, y, and z coordinates.
For example, in the first octant, all coordinates are positive (x > 0, y > 0, z > 0).

flashcards.title: Linear Programming Problems
explanation: Linear programming problems involve finding the maximum or minimum value of a linear function (called the objective function) subject to constraints expressed as linear inequalities.
The variables in the problem are non-negative and satisfy the constraints.

flashcards.title: Objective Function
formulas: Z = ax + by
explanation: The objective function is a linear expression of decision variables, which is maximized or minimized according to the given problem.

flashcards.title: Constraints
explanation: Constraints are the restrictions on the decision variables, expressed as inequalities.
Non-negative restrictions ensure that x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.

flashcards.title: Feasible Region and Feasible Solution
explanation: The feasible region is the common region determined by all constraints, including non-negative constraints.
A feasible solution is any point within or on the boundary of the feasible region that satisfies all constraints.

flashcards.title: Optimal Solution
explanation: An optimal solution is a point in the feasible region that gives the maximum or minimum value of the objective function.
The optimal value occurs at a corner point of the feasible region (Theorem 1).

flashcards.title: Different Types of Linear Programming Problems
explanation: Manufacturing Problems: Determine the number of units to produce for maximum profit while meeting resource constraints.
Diet Problems: Minimize the cost of a diet while meeting minimum nutritional requirements.
Transportation Problems: Optimize transportation schedules to minimize costs while meeting supply and demand.

flashcards.title: Formulation of LPP
explanation: Formulate the problem as a mathematical model with an objective function, constraints, and non-negative restrictions.
Identify decision variables and express constraints as linear inequalities.

flashcards.title: Solving LPP
explanation: Plot constraints to determine the feasible region.
Identify corner points of the feasible region and substitute them into the objective function to find the optimal solution.
If the feasible region is unbounded, check whether an optimal value exists at infinity.

flashcards.title: Conditional Probability
formulas: P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F) / P(F), P(F) ≠ 0
explanation: Conditional probability is the probability of event E occurring given that event F has already occurred.
It is defined as the ratio of the probability of the intersection of E and F to the probability of F.

flashcards.title: Multiplication Theorem on Probability
formulas: P(E ∩ F) = P(E) × P(F|E)
explanation: The probability of two events E and F occurring together is the product of the probability of E and the conditional probability of F given E.

flashcards.title: Independent Events
formulas: P(E ∩ F) = P(E) × P(F)
explanation: Two events E and F are independent if the occurrence of one does not affect the occurrence of the other.
If E and F are independent, then P(F|E) = P(F) and P(E|F) = P(E).

flashcards.title: Bayes' Theorem
formulas: P(Ei|A) = [P(Ei) × P(A|Ei)] / Σ[P(Ej) × P(A|Ej)]
explanation: Bayes' theorem is used to find the probability of an event Ei given that another event A has occurred.
It relates conditional probabilities with prior probabilities and likelihood.

flashcards.title: Random Variable
explanation: A random variable is a real-valued function that assigns numerical values to outcomes of a random experiment.
Random variables can be discrete or continuous.

flashcards.title: Mean and Variance of Random Variable
formulas: Mean: μ = Σ[xi × P(xi)]
Variance: Var(X) = Σ[(xi - μ)² × P(xi)]
explanation: The mean (or expected value) is the weighted average of all possible values of a random variable.
The variance measures the spread of the values around the mean.

flashcards.title: Bernoulli Trials
explanation: A Bernoulli trial is a random experiment with exactly two outcomes: success and failure.
The probability of success is constant for each trial, and trials are independent.

flashcards.title: Binomial Distribution
explanation: The binomial distribution gives the probability of exactly r successes in n independent Bernoulli trials.
Here, p is the probability of success and (1-p) is the probability of failure.
